ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF
JUSTICE

Small Claims Court

BETWEEN:

BARRY HALES

Plaintiff

– and –

Niagara neighbourhood housing
co-operative inc., patricia antoine,
and
arlene ludlow

Defendants

Kamin, Rhea

Matunin-Brown, Jennifer and

Baxter, Nicholas

HEARD in Toronto:

March 1 and 2, 2018

JUDGMENT

[
1
]

The plaintiff, Barry Hales, is a 72-year old man with 50 years
experience in property management, 14 of which are in the cooperative housing
sector.  The defendant, Niagara Neighbourhood Housing Co-Operative Inc. (the
“Co-Op”), hired Mr. Hales to be its Property Manager.

[
2
]

Mr. Hales worked for the Co-Op from June to October 2016, a period
of 3 months, 22 days, with annual compensation of $43,000, a four-day work-week
of 28 hours, and Fridays off.  As part of his key duties, Mr. Hales was tasked
with contacting individuals, on waiting lists administered by the City of
Toronto, to become tenants of the Co-Op, and advising them of an opportunity to
be interviewed and become a member of the Co-Op if they met eligibility
requirements.   He worked closely with members of the Board of Directors, who
ultimately made the decision of who would be a new tenant/member of the Co-Op.
Mr. Hales was terminated for cause early in October 2016.  In April 2017, he
commenced this wrongful dismissal claim, claiming $25,000 from the defendants.

[
3
]

At the beginning of trial for his wrongful dismissal claim, Mr.
Hales dropped his claims against the individual defendants, Ms. Antoine and Ms.
Ludlow.  At the request of the individual defendants, I reserved on the issue
of costs.  These individual defendants were the main witnesses for the Co-Op.

[
4
]

As there was no written contract of employment, Mr. Hales would be
entitled to common law reasonable notice of termination or pay in lieu of such
notice, if his employment was terminated without cause.  However, if the Co-Op
is able to establish cause, then the Co-Op would be justified in having
terminated him without notice or pay in lieu of notice.

[
5
]

The following were the issues against the Co-Op at trial:

(a)

Was there
cause to terminate Mr. Hales’ employment?

(b)

If
not, what is the appropriate period of reasonable notice?

(c)

Is Mr. Hales entitled to be paid for the expenses he claims were
incurred while he was employed by the Co-Op?

(d)

Is an
award of punitive or aggravated damages appropriate?

[
6
]

The law is well established: where an indefinite term employee is
terminated without notice and for cause, the burden is on the employer to establish
or prove the “for cause” termination.

[
7
]

I find, based on the evidence of witnesses and the preponderance
of probabilities in this case, that the employer, the Co-Op, has established
cause for such termination.

[
8
]

I

also find that the plaintiff has not shown on a balance of probabilities that
he is entitled to reimbursement of his claimed expenses.  Given my conclusion
on the key issues, an award of punitive or aggravated damages is not
appropriate.

[
9
]

My reasons for this conclusion follow.

EVIDENCE

[
10
]

I reserved
judgment on March 2, 2018, so I could review the materials and evidence.  At
the request of the defendant, and by agreement of the plaintiff, the plaintiff forwarded

copies of his personal
and corporate income tax returns
to this Court after the conclusion of this
trial to show what income he earned over the relevant period.

[
11
]

Mr. Hales gave evidence, and
also called Jan Griffiths, Ankica (Anna) Tirca, and Muhammad Rehman as his
witnesses. The plaintiff also submitted an unsigned declaration from Ms. Thien
Binh Pham, a candidate for potential membership into the Co-Op, which I
ultimately did not consider.

[
12
]

The defendant Co-Op called
Arlene Dawne Ludlow, Rudolph C. Klein, Patricia Antoine, and Robert Ross as its
witnesses.   Ms. Ludlow, Mr. Klein and Ms. Antoine are all volunteer directors
for the Co-Op, whereas Mr. Ross is the Co-Op’s maintenance coordinator.

[
13
]

I also reviewed the
plaintiff’s three volume document brief, and the Co-Op’s one volume document
brief.

General Conduct

[
14
]

I start with a review of evidence related
to the background of this case, and Mr. Hales general conduct on the job.

[
15
]

Mr. Hales stated that he applied to the
Co-Op for the position of Property Manager.  He described, as part of his
responsibilities, working closely with members of the Co-Op’s Board and
attending the monthly board meetings.  He confirmed that his responsibilities
included preparing the agendas for these monthly board meetings, presenting two
reports for each Board meeting, making sure that all late payments were
collected, and also keeping the units at the Co-Op occupied.  He was also
responsible for preparing the Rent Geared Income and Operational Review reports
for the Co-Op, as required by the City of Toronto.  He believed that the
relationship between himself and the Board, especially Ms. Patricia Antoine
with whom he dealt mostly, was fine until the end of September 2016.

[
16
]

He admitted working on
his wife’s immigration matter while at work, including
having discussions with his local Member of Parliament, but he believed that
doing this should not have been an issue, since he said this took up no more
than an hour a week.

[
17
]

Ms.
Arlene Dawne Ludlow is a resident of the
Co-Op, and the Director of Membership for its Board.  In this capacity, she
interacted with Mr. Hales, when he set up meetings of prospective tenants for
the Co-Op with Board members responsible for conducting interviews.  She
testified about her concerns that Mr. Hales had been in a conflict of interest
when he arranged for Ms. Pham’s interview with members of the Board, ahead of
six others on the official City of Toronto list.  She was also concerned when
Ms. Pham stated during the interview that she knew Mr. Hales personally and
that he had visited her apartment.  When she asked Mr. Hales the day after the
interview about Ms. Pham’s statements, he denied he knew her personally or that
he visited her apartment. Ms. Ludlow told Ms. Antoine, another board member,
about her concerns.

[
18
]

Ms. Ludlow also recalled seeing Mr. Hales
handling his wife’s immigration application during work hours, and that she
told him to work on it during his day off.

[
19
]

Patricia Antoine, a self-identified Black
woman, and a member of the Board and the Staff Liaison, as well as Chair of the
Selection Committee, at the relevant time, worked closely with Mr. Hales. She
was able to observe his work ethic, and she found it unsatisfactory. She found
that he was often attending to personal matters during his work hours.  Mr.
Hales had told her about marrying a woman in the Philippines and he was trying
to get her into Canada. He told her that he had to call the Philippines at
night and was tired during the day.  On several occasions, she had noticed him
asleep or falling asleep, including on one occasion when the Co-Op’s auditor was
present, and that he often kept his office door closed.  She advised him many
times that he had to keep his door wide open, during office hours. Ms. Antoine
also said that Mr. Hales did not take direction well from her.  She would talk
to him, and he would always be muttering or upset.

[
20
]

She was also concerned that Mr. Hales had
told her that he liked Asian people, and that he could tell by the names of the
list of potential candidates to join the Co-Op community who were the Asian
ones.  When Ms. Ludlow told her about Ms. Pham, Ms. Antoine thought Mr. Hales
might be favouring Asian candidates to become tenants of the Co-Op, which was
not permitted.  Candidates were to be interviewed in the order that they
appeared on the official list.

[
21
]

Although there were times when they were
able to work well together, Ms. Antoine noticed that she had increasing
difficulty working with Mr. Hales starting sometime in September, when his wife
was denied entry into Canada.  He came to work upset, and treated Ms. Antoine like
she was the one responsible, as if she was from Immigration Canada.  He would
suddenly get agitated, and he would start swearing “fucking bullshit”,
particularly when she asked him to make sure to send in the reports for the
Co-Op on time.

[
22
]

Robert Ross is the
maintenance coordinator for the Co-Op.  He also testified that Mr. Hales was
often engaged in non-work activities, including being on the phone for
immigration issues. He could hear that it related to legal issues and bringing
someone into Canada, but did not listen in long on Mr. Hales’ calls.

[
23
]

Rudoph C. Klein is the President of the
Board of the Co-Op.   Mr. Klein did not have much interaction with Mr. Hales,
but he does recall that during Mr. Hales’ tenure as the Property Manager, he
received many more emails and calls from the City’s Social Housing
representative than he normally would, related to paperwork that was overdue.
Mr. Klein said that he asked Mr. Hales to prioritize his work, but that
although Mr. Hales kept saying that he was working on the paperwork, he failed
to complete it.

“Fucking Slave” Comment

[
24
]

According to Mr. Hales, on
September 30, 2016, which would have been a Friday, Ms. Antoine appeared in his
office and questioned him about his favouring Asians over other potential residents
for the Co-Op.  He denied doing this.  He stated this was not the first time
that Ms. Antoine had questioned him about his choice of tenants, and in fact
she had been asking for a few days.  He admitted that he “lost it” that day and
told her he was not her “fucking slave”.  He recalled that it was only the two
of them in the inner office when he made this comment, and that no one else was
present.

[
25
]

Ms. Antoine testified that
she recalled entering Mr. Hales’ office to speak to him about his late reports,
and concerns about his failure to follow Board policies regarding Co-Op
membership and choice of candidates.  He not only refused to provide her with
any information, but he said he was not her  “fucking slave”, and he suddenly
started yelling at her, very upset.

She,
as a Black woman, was very offended by the
“fucking slave” comment, but she kept her calm.

[
26
]

Unlike Mr. Hales, Ms. Antoine
remembers this incident happened on Wednesday, October 5, 2016.

[
27
]

Mr. Ross, whose office is
about ten feet away from Mr. Hales’ office, recalls overhearing Mr. Hales
raising his voice against Ms. Antoine.  This was highly unusual, and,
concerned, he went over to Mr. Hales’ office to see what was going on.  He is
uncertain on what date this happened.

[
28
]

Ms. Ludlow also recalls going
to Mr. Hales’ office, also out of concern when she heard his loud voice.  However,
her evidence is that she also had a confrontation with Mr. Hales earlier that
day, and the “fucking slave” comment to Ms. Antoine came after her own
confrontation with him.

October 5,
2016 and “Bedbug” Problems

[
29
]

According to Mr. Hales, on
October 5, 2016, which would have been a Wednesday, he had a tense discussion
with Ms. Ludlow, who was upset about bedbugs in the Co-Op, and his failure to
follow procedure in handling bedbug issues in the Co-op, which he denied.  Ms.
Ludlow “threw him out of a job” and demanded, then grabbed, his office keys from
him and told him to go home. He believed that he had been terminated from his
job, and he left the office.

Mr. Hales denies that the “fucking slave” incident happened on this day.

[
30
]

Both Ms. Ludlow and Ms.
Antoine have a starkly different view of what happened on October 5, 2016:

(a)

Ms.
Ludlow testified that she had always
worked closely with the Property Manager, and in this case, with Mr. Hales.  On
October 5, 2016, she had gone to his office to speak to him about a problem
with bedbugs.  She remembered the date because the Co-Op had its pest control
person visit that day.  Mr. Hales told her that the bedbugs were in the unit
next to hers and that the occupant had refused entry to pest control.  Ms.
Ludlow told Mr. Hales that he must alert the Board immediately if any resident
refuses entry, as bedbugs were a serious issue, which could easily spread
throughout the Co-Op.  She testified that Mr. Hales grew agitated when she told
him what procedure to follow, and he said:  “I don’t give a shit”, and “I don’t
have to fucking tell you anything”. Ms. Ludlow left and returned to her unit.
Not long after, she heard Mr. Hales screaming.  She returned to his office, to
see Mr. Hales flicking papers and yelling at Ms. Antoine. She heard Mr. Hales
say “I am not your fucking slave”.

(b)

Ms. Ludlow denied that Mr. Hales was
terminated from his employment that day, since any decision to terminate his
employment would have to be made by unanimous decision of the Board.  Given his
state, they told him to leave for the day and the Board would contact him.  She
said that no one grabbed keys from Mr. Hales.  He was very upset, and he threw
his own keys down on his desk. He then tried to take papers out of the office.

(c)

As
noted above, Ms. Antoine also recalls the “fucking slave” comment to have
occurred on October 5, 2016, and not September 30, 2016.
Ms. Antoine also described her meeting
with Mr. Hales to discuss work issues, which escalated into Mr. Hales saying to
her that he is “not a personal slave”, that this was none of her “fucking
business” and to leave him alone, and going so far as saying “fuck you” and
“fuck off”.
She was also afraid that he would
physically strike her, because he was very agitated.
She described him
as “in my face”, pointing at her and accusing her of challenging him.

(d)

Ms. Antoine also said that
Mr. Hales was not terminated on October 5, and that such a decision could only
be made by the Board.  She also said that Mr. Hales threw his keys on the desk
himself, and confirmed both Mr. Ross and Ms. Ludlow separately also showed up
in Mr. Hales’ office concerned about his yelling.

[
31
]

Mr. Ross

testified that he intervened when he heard a commotion and Mr. Hales’ loud
voice coming from his office, which was about 10 feet away his own office.  He
confirmed hearing Mr. Hales say “I am not your fucking slave”.  When he walked into
Mr. Hales’ office to investigate, Ms. Antoine asked if he had heard everything
and he confirmed that he did.  He also heard Ms. Antoine asking Mr. Hales about
government papers that were past due, and recalled that Mr. Hales was very
angry and his anger was directed at Ms. Antoine
.
He recalled Mr. Hales
feeling justified in being so upset.

[
32
]

However, unlike Ms. Antoine
and Ms. Ludlow, Mr. Ross conceded during cross-examination that he was
uncertain of when this occurred.  He said that it could have happened a couple
of days prior to the October 6, 2016 meeting of the board, or one to two weeks
prior to the meeting.

He said that he was the one that signed the work
orders for pest control, and he confirmed that it looked like he signed the
work order dated October 6, 2016.  However, he also said that it is possible
that pest control attended the Co-Op on October 5, 2016.

Board Meeting
on October 6, 2016

[
33
]

Mr. Klein explained that he arranged the Thursday,
October 6, 2016, special meeting of the Board so that the Board members could
all decide what to do about Mr. Hale’s behaviour.  This was not a regular
monthly board meeting, but one that he specially scheduled, after Ms. Ludlow
and Mr. Ross raised concerns about Mr. Hales’ swearing and behaviour. He may
have written notes, and he may have thrown away the notes, but he is not sure
what happened.  Since the meeting was not the usual monthly board meeting, and
it was called to deal with Mr. Hales’ conduct, he may also have believed that
it would be confidential and no minutes would be required, as they would not be
circulated.

[
34
]

Mr. Ross also said that this was not a
regular board meeting, and that he was asked to attend to answer questions
about Mr. Hales’ behaviour.  After providing the responses, which were the same
as the responses he provided during the trial, he was asked to leave.

[
35
]

According to Mr. Hales, during this
meeting, he
claims to have apologized for cursing at
Ms. Antoine.  He says he was then asked to step out and when he came back into
the meeting, he was told that his employment was terminated.  Mr. Hales said
that the board simply confirmed the decision from the day before, and that he
was not told that he had been terminated for cause.  Although he asked if he
should go over any agenda items for the October 11, 2016 scheduled board
meeting, he was told that was not necessary.

[
36
]

Ms. Ludlow, Ms. Antoine, and Mr. Klein
have a very different recollection of what happened during this special meeting
of the Board.  None of them recall Mr. Hales apologizing for his behaviour.

(a)

Ms. Ludlow recalled Mr. Hales stating,
after being asked about his conduct, that he felt justified and he would
“fucking do it again”. She also stated that, after Mr. Hales left the room, the
Board’s general consensus was that Mr. Hales’ employment had to be terminated
for cause, but that he would be offered two weeks pay if he apologized.  When
the Board told Mr. Hales of its decision, he told them “I do not need this
fucking shit”, and threatened that the Board would hear from his lawyer.  After
he refused the two weeks offer, he was terminated for cause.

(b)

Ms. Antoine also recalled that Mr. Hales
justified his actions, and said he would “f’ing” do it again if he had a
chance.

(c)

Mr. Klein stated
that during the meeting, Mr. Hales did not deny his conduct, and justified his
behaviour as not being “in a good mood”.  He recalled that the decision was to
terminate Mr. Hales’ conduct, and that the Board told him the reason for the
termination related to his unacceptable conduct.

Other Witnesses

[
37
]

The evidence from Mr. Hales’
other witnesses did not touch on the key issues.  Their evidence is briefly
summarized:

(a)

Jan Griffiths worked for the Co-Op for
two years between October 2012 to October 2014.  She had no  evidence that
related to Mr. Hales directly.  I did not find that her general evidence about
the performance of property management duties in the period between October
2012 to Otober 2014 was relevant and I gave no weight to it.

(b)

Ankica (Anna) Tirca worked in property
management for 19 years, and had been a property manager in co-operative
housing for 8 years.  She appeared to have been called to give evidence about
the workload that Mr. Hales would have had while employed at the Co-Op.  She
gave evidence that she worked at the Co-Op from October 2016 to the end of
January 2017, a period of about four (4) months, starting immediately after Mr.
Hales’ employment was terminated.  She worked 20 to 25 hour weeks, depending on
her other work commitments.  She testified that when she started working, the
AGI and operational reviews had not been finished and she knew that they were
late.  She prioritized these and did the bulk of the work in two weeks, but
approvals and implementations with the City was an ongoing process.  She
completed them in January 2017.

(c)

Muhammed Rehman
was called to speak to the likely date of the “fucking slave” incident, which
the plaintiff’s counsel submitted when to credibility.  Mr. Rehman is an
entomologist, and the owner of First Choice, the pest control business
regularly used by the Co-Op. In reviewing Exhibit no. 6, he acknowledged that
these were work tickets dated September 1, September 21, October 6, and October
14, 2018, for visits to the Co-Op. In October 2016, he testified that in
addition to the regular visit on October 6, 2016, he had been called on October
14, 2016 to visit a particular unit.  He stated that if there is no work ticket
for October 5, then pest control work would not have been done on that day.

Expenses Claim

[
38
]

Mr. Hales also claimed that he paid for
expenses on behalf of the Co-Op and he was entitled to reimbursement.

[
39
]

The Co-Op denied any obligation to
reimburse Mr. Hales for these expenses. Ms. Antoine said that the Co-Op has
people they use to fix computers, they have a Staples card from which they
could simply order products online, and there was always a petty cash supply of
$300.  Mr. Hales would not have been expected to use his own funds to purchase
anything for the Co-Op.  She also stated that the Co-Op does not have any of
the items that Mr. Hales claimed to have purchased, and that they would never
have asked him to purchase any air conditioner units, or fans or heaters.

Conclusion

[
40
]

Based on the evidence, I find
that the following incidents have been proven on a balance of probabilities:

(a)

Mr.
Hales told Ms. Antoine that he was not her “fucking slave”.  He also cursed and
raised his voice at Ms. Antoine.  This finding is based on testimony given by
Ms. Ludlow, Ms. Antoine and Mr. Ross.

(b)

Although
there is some dispute when he was actually terminated, whether on October 5 or
October 6, the fact is that Mr. Hales understood that he had been terminated
from his employment on October 5, 2017, and the Board of Directors confirmed it
on October 6, 2017. Given both the testimony of Ms. Ludlow and Ms. Antoine that
only the Board could make the decision to terminate Mr. Hales’ employment, and
Mr. Klein’s evidence that the meeting was called specially to discuss Mr.
Hales’ behaviour, the preponderance of evidence indicates that the termination
formally occurred at the specially called meeting of the Board on October 6,
2017.

(c)

Mr.
Hales did not produce reports in a timely manner.  This may have been affected
by the time that he spent on his wife’s application, and then then the denial
of his wife’s entry into Canada, which distracted him and also affected his
attention to the report production.  Ms. Ludlow, Ms. Antoine and Mr. Ross all
gave evidence of Mr. Hales’ preoccupation with his wife’s immigration
situation.  Ms. Antoine and Mr. Klein both gave evidence that Mr. Hales’
reports were late.  Ms. Tirca confirmed that the reports were not done when she
took over Mr. Hales’ Property Manager position.

[
41
]

Considerable
time was spent on allegations regarding Mr. Hales’ favouritism of certain
potential tenants over others higher on the official list, and the process to
determine who would occupy vacant units at the Co-Op. The Co-Op’s evidence on
this point was that Mr. Hales tried to have Ms. Pham become a member of the
Co-Op, and arranged for her to be interviewed in advance of others that were higher
up on the list.  Ms. Ludlow testified that during her interview of Ms. Pham,
she had said that she knew Mr. Hales personally and that he had visited her
apartment.  Both Ms. Ludlow and Ms Antoine said that this was inconsistent with
the expected behaviour of a Property Manager.  Mr. Hales produced an unsigned
statement from Ms. Pham, denying that she knew Mr. Hales personally or that he
ever visited her apartment.  This issue did not factor into my determination of
the case, and I make no findings on this issue.

ANALYSIS

[
42
]

I am mindful of the principle of
proceedings before the Small Claims Court provided by section 25 of
the
Courts of Justice Act
:

Summary
hearings

25

The
Small Claims Court shall hear and determine in a summary way all questions of law
and fact and may make such order as is considered just and agreeable to good
conscience.

I have tried to
be brief in these reasons, and to highlight only the relevant evidence.

[
43
]

The
law is well established: where an employee for an indefinite term is terminated
for cause and without notice, the burden is on the employer to establish or
prove the “for cause” termination.

[
44
]

In
the case of
McKinley v. BC Tel
,
2001 SCC 38 (CanLII)
,

the Supreme Court of Canada set out the
appropriate test in paragraphs 48 and 49 to determine whether just cause exists
in a given situation.

The Supreme
Court confirmed that a contextual approach of the alleged misconduct, leading
to a termination for cause, is required:

…. I am of the view that
whether an employer is justified in dismissing an employee on the grounds of
dishonesty is a question that requires an assessment of the context of the
alleged misconduct. More specifically,

the test is whether the employee’s dishonesty gave rise to a breakdown
in the employment relationship
. This test can be
expressed in different ways. One could say, for example, that just cause for
dismissal exists where the dishonesty violates an essential condition of the
employment contract, breaches the faith inherent to the work relationship, or is
fundamentally or directly inconsistent with the employee’s obligations to his
or her employer.

In accordance with this
test, a trial judge must instruct the jury to determine:

(1) whether the evidence established the employee’s deceitful conduct
on a balance of probabilities; and (2) if so, whether the nature and degree of
the dishonesty warranted dismissal.

In my view, the second branch of this test does not
blend questions of fact and law. Rather, assessing the seriousness of the
misconduct requires the facts established at trial to be carefully considered
and balanced. As such, it is a factual inquiry for the jury to undertake.

[emphasis added]

[
45
]

The
application of
McKinley
is not restricted to dishonest or deceitful
conduct.  Subsequent cases have applied this test in circumstances involving
serious misconduct such as insubordination and insolence, and assessing whether
the seriousness of the misconduct “is reconcilable with sustaining the
employment relationship”.

[
46
]

Using
the analysis found in
McKinley
,
first, I must determine:

(a)

Whether
the evidence establishes that Mr. Hales’ misconduct has been proved on a
balance of probabilities; and

(b)

If so,
I must consider the nature and degree of the misconduct against the contextual
background to assess whether the termination for cause was warranted.  For
that, I would consider whether the misconduct warranted immediate dismissal
because it gave rise to a breakdown in the employment relationship, in that it
violated an essential condition of the employment contract, breached the faith
inherent to the work relationship or was otherwise fundamentally or directly
inconsistent with Mr. Hale’s obligation to the Co-Op.

[
47
]

Contrary to a closing
submission made by the plaintiff’s counsel, there is no evidence to support the
allegation that the Co-Op sought to “trump up allegations of cause” against Mr.
Hales.  The main evidence of the witnesses for the Co-Op, Ms. Ludlow, Mr.
Klein, Ms. Antoine and Mr. Ross, is generally consistent and remained
consistent through cross-examination.  While there may be inconsistencies on
some factual issues, in particular on dates of when incidents occurred, I find
the contradictory accounts of what happened on what dates to be consistent with
vagaries in memory rather than in deliberate mischaracterization or
misrepresentation of the facts.   The key details and the Co-Op’s witnesses’
concerns about Mr. Hales are the same or similar.  As for the dates, September
30 is a Friday, and October 5 is the following Wednesday.  There is no dispute
that the meeting of the Board occurred on Thursday, October 6, 2016.   This is
a span of less than one week, in the lives of three witnesses who are all
volunteer directors of the Board, and in the case of the maintenance
coordinator, who was not kept abreast at the time of what was happening.  Even
if the “fucking slave” incident did occur on September 30, the Board could only
meet on October 6 to decide what to do about Mr. Hales’ employment.

[
48
]

I find that the Co-Op was
able to establish cause based on Mr. Hales’ response to Ms. Antoine that he was
not her “fucking slave”, and his aggressive swearing and loud voice, which drew
the attention of both Mr. Ross and Ms. Ludlow to his office.  His comments and
attitude occurred after Ms. Antoine asked him legitimate questions about late
reports and other work issues, or possibly, as Mr. Hales claims, after she
questioned him about favouritism shown to Ms. Pham.  In any of these
situations, such a response and attitude towards a Board member that he
regularly reports to is offensive and a form of misconduct warranting
dismissal.

[
49
]

The fact that Mr. Hales made
the comment about being a “fucking slave” to Ms. Antoine, who self-identifies
as a visibly Black woman, is particularly appalling in light of the history of
slavery in North America.  Mr. Hales knew or should have known that such a
comment would have been offensive to Ms. Antoine.  Ms. Antoine testified that
she was very offended by the comment.

[
50
]

Further, this comment was
made in the context of ongoing issues relating to Mr. Hales’ performance as a
Property Manager, and questions about his integrity.
I have found that the
comment itself, and the context and attitude he had when making the comments
themselves (“fucking slave”, “fuck you”, etc), were sufficient to ground cause
for termination.  However, if the offensive comment and attitude directed at
Ms. Antoine is not sufficient for summary termination of his employment, I have
also found that the combination of his offensive comment and attitude to Ms.
Antoine and Mr. Hales’ justification of his conduct during the Board meeting
does constitute cause for termination.  The evidence from the Co-Op’s witnesses
established that Mr. Hales had not only been offensive and insolent, but also
insubordinate, and he refused to recognize his own misconduct. Although Mr.
Hales claims to have apologized for his behaviour, based on a balance of
probabilities from the evidence of other witnesses, Mr. Hales justified his
behaviour, and his behaviour ruptured the employment relationship.

[
51
]

Mr. Hales does not have
the kind of lengthy service record with the Co-Op, which the Co-Op would have
been obliged to consider in determining the appropriate sanction.  He was a
less than ideal employee of less than four months.  He was not induced away
from other employment to take on the Property Manager position.  His
conduct, in short time,
became incompatible with continued employment with the Co-Op.

[
52
]

I have
relied on the case of
Wise v. Broadway Properties Ltd
.,
2005 BCCA 546
(CanLII)
, in which the British Columbia Court of Appeal affirmed a trial
judge’s decision that an employer was justified in terminating the 10-year
employment of a resident caretaker of an apartment block.  The trial decision
was premised on the caretaker having sent a written anti-Semitic remark to one
of the principals of the business, along with a threat to sue.  The remark
consisted of a statement that he did “not expect to be treated as the
unfortunate Jews were treated when impressed into working without pay… during the
Second World War.”

[
53
]

In
upholding the trial judge’s dismissal of the plaintiff’s wrongful dismissal
action, Justice Donald of the Court of Appeal noted in paragraph 20 that:

In my view the decision can be upheld solely on the finding in
connection with the insult, without reference to the threat, if that is what it
was.  I prefer not to express an opinion on that aspect of the case.  The trial
judge’s conclusion about the effect of the insult on the employment
relationship is bound up in his appreciation of the evidence and it is not
palpably wrong.

[
54
]

I have also relied on the case of
Mellquist v. Lake of the
Rivers No. 72 (Rural Municipality),

[1987] S.J. No. 780
, which involved a
foreman with ten years service.    In the last year of his employment, he
became dissatisfied, failing to complete projects in timely manner, and
wilfully refusing to obey orders given to him.  The foreman also deliberately shortened
the work week of his crew, notwithstanding that a project was already behind
schedule.   The defendant terminated his employment for cause.  At page 5 of
the judgment:

Insolence towards one’s employer, fellow
employees, or members of the public, when acting in one’s scope of employment
are all just cause for dismissal.

Insolence is defined in Webster’s New
International Dictionary as “haughty and contemptuous or brutal behaviour
language; lacking usual or proper respect for rank or position; presumptuously
disrespectful or familiar towards equals or superiors”.

It was a whole series of events or course of
conduct between the middle of the year 1985 and September 12
th
, 1986
that led to the plaintiff’s dismissal.  Not one event was the sole cause.

[
55
]

The
events of October 6 are not meaningless, as Ms. Kamin suggests.  The meeting of
the board was not a regular meeting.  It was called specifically to deal with
Mr. Hale’s conduct.  Ms. Kamin requested that I make an adverse finding based
on meeting minutes either having been destroyed or missing.  I decline to make
such a finding. Mr. Klein testified that he did not think that the notes were
important, since this was not a regular meeting of the Board.  While it would
have been better to have written notes, I am satisfied based on the evidence of
Mr. Hales, Ms. Antoine, Ms. Ludlow, Mr. Klein and Mr. Ross about what happened
at the meeting of the Board.  Where their evidence contradicted the evidence of
Mr. Hales, I preferred their more consistent evidence that Mr. Hales remained
recalcitrant about his conduct.

[
56
]

On the issue of whether Mr.
Hales is entitled to have his claimed expenses reimbursed, I find that Mr.
Hales has not proven that he is entitled to reimbursement.  He was unable to
produce receipts for the list of expenses that he submitted as an exhibit.
Although he claimed to have incurred these expenses for the Co-Op, the Co-Op
denied that it received any of the items listed.  As such, Mr. Hales has failed
to prove on a balance of probabilities that he is entitled to reimbursement.

Appropriate period of reasonable notice

[
57
]

If I am
wrong in finding that there was cause to terminate Mr. Hales’ employment, I
would otherwise have considered the usual factors in determining common law
reasonable notice, as found in
Bardal v Globe
& Mail Ltd.

(
1960),
1960 CanLII 294 (ON SC)
,
24
DLR (2d) 140
, and
expanded by subsequent decisions.

[
58
]

These factors would have
included Mr. Hales’ age (72 years old), the nature of his employment, his brief
tenure of just under four months, and the availability of similar employment.
I also considered that, although he alleged inducement, he was in fact
unemployed at the time of his hire and he applied for the job with the Co-Op.

[
59
]

I find that an appropriate
period of reasonable notice is three months, less any amounts already paid or
income earned during this period.  Age alone, without some length of tenure,
does not entitle Mr. Hales to a reasonable notice period of eight months, as
the plaintiff sought in the Statement of Claim, or the six months that the
plaintiff’s counsel pleaded in submissions at trial.

Aggravated and
Punitive Damages

[
60
]

Further, even if I had not
found that cause was proven, I would not have awarded aggravated or punitive
damages.

[
61
]

Any award
of aggravated damages is compensatory in nature.  It requires a proof of injury
aggravated by the defendants’ conduct, entitling the plaintiff to additional
compensation.  By contrast, punitive damages are awarded to punish a
defendant’s egregious conduct.

[
62
]

Mr. Hales has led no evidence
or insufficient evidence regarding any aggravated injury caused by the Co-Op’s
decision to terminate his employment.

[
63
]

Further, punitive damages are
very much the exception rather than the rule, and should only be granted where
there has been high-handed, malicious, arbitrary or highly reprehensible
misconduct, departing markedly from the ordinary standards of decent
behaviour.

[
64
]

Even if I had not found cause,
there was a reasonable basis for the Co-Op’s termination for cause.  I do not
find that the Co-Op’s conduct has been high-handed, malicious, arbitrary or
highly reprehensible such that the conduct departs to a marked degree from
ordinary standards of decent behaviour.  The evidence showed that Mr. Hales was
not an ideal employee.

[
65
]

I would have found that Mr.
Hales had not made out his case for punitive or aggravated damages.

DISPOSITION

[
66
]

After hearing the testimony of the
witnesses and reviewing the exhibits the submissions of counsel,
based on a preponderance of the evidence,
I find that the Co-Op was justified in terminating Mr.
Hales’ employment.

[
67
]

The onus was on the Co-Op to show cause.
The Co-Op was able to establish misconduct, and the preponderance of evidence
indicated that Mr. Hales felt his conduct was justified.  In the particular
context in which the misconduct occurred, Mr. Hales had ruptured the employment
relationship.

[
68
]

In the circumstances, the
plaintiff’s claim is dismissed.

COSTS

[
69
]

The plaintiff made a late withdrawal of
the claims against the individual defendants, Patricia Antoine and Arlene
Ludlow, the morning of trial.
I allowed the withdrawal of the claim against
the individual defendants, but stated that costs would be dealt with at the end
of the trial.  The defendants’ counsel indicated that significant costs had
been incurred to prepare the defence for the two individual defendants, even if
the claims were then withdrawn at the opening of trial.

[
70
]

Costs
ordinarily follow the event.  I urge the parties to agree on costs payable by
the plaintiff to the Co-Op and the two individual defendants against whom the
claim was withdrawn at the beginning of trial.  The parties should consider the
appropriate level of costs, taking into consideration two days of trial, the
fact that the late withdrawal of the claim against the two individual
defendants led to increased fees, and, significantly, the plaintiff’s ability
to pay costs.

[
71
]

If efforts to
agree on costs prove unsuccessful, the parties may seek an appointment before
me to make costs submissions.
